# Why the protestors behind the woman in white all face the same way near the end

## What the clip is

The video is a Democracy Broadcasting.TV item from the 13 March 2018 demonstration against President Trump's visit to Southern California — the opening caption states it: "Left-wing groups organized protest to Pres. Trump's appearance in So. California – March 13, 2018". The location is the lawn of Beverly Gardens Park where it runs alongside Santa Monica Boulevard in Beverly Hills; the illuminated "BEVERLY HILLS" city sign is visible behind the crowd in the closing shots.

The woman in white is not part of the crowd behind her. Captioned "Ms. Ogo James — Nigerian stands-up against Trump-detractors", her hand-lettered board reads "#CALIFORNIA4TRUMP / #BLACKS4TRUMP / #BEVERLYHILLS4TRUMP / #WOMEN4TRUMP / #WOMEN4MELANIA4TRUMP / 4TRUMP WHO CAN BE AGAINST HIM / GOD BLESS TRUMP, GOD BLESS AMERICA". She is a lone pro-Trump counter-demonstrator being interviewed in the middle of an anti-Trump rally. The people behind her are the rally: "Impeach", "Traitor", "HATE HAS NO HOME HERE!", "WALL PRIORITY?" placards, pink pussyhat flags, and a small Trump effigy in a suit and red tie.

## The answer

For almost the whole 5½ minutes the camera is locked in tight close-up on her face, so the background is only ever a soft scatter of people drifting about the lawn in all directions. In the last fifteen seconds or so — roughly 305 s to the fade-out at about 321 s — the operator pulls back and swings round, and the wide shot finally reveals the geometry of the protest: the demonstrators are not scattered at all. They are strung out in a line along the edge of the park where it meets Santa Monica Boulevard, and every one of them is turned outward toward the roadway. Car headlights and motorcycles are visible streaming past on the right-hand side of the frame at 318–321 s.

**They all face the same direction because that is what a roadside picket is.** The demonstrators line the kerb and point their placards outward at the passing traffic so that drivers on a major Beverly Hills thoroughfare can read them, and so they can draw honks and waves of support. A protest sign only works if it is aimed at an audience, so everyone holding one naturally orients the same way — toward the street. Nothing has happened at that moment to summon their attention: there is no speaker, no stage, no confrontation and no police line in shot. The shared orientation was there all along; it is the camera pulling back that makes it visible for the first time, and a line of people seen end-on reads as one solid block all looking the same way.

Three further factors reinforce the effect at exactly that point in the video:

1. **The camera and the interview are on the street side of the line.** The news camera, the hand-held microphone and other bystanders' phones — one person is clearly visible at the right of frame around 307–315 s holding a smartphone up in both hands to film — are all positioned between the crowd and the road. So "facing the traffic" and "facing the camera" are very nearly the same direction here.

2. **Some of them deliberately gather into the shot.** Between about 309 s and 318 s the group carrying the "WALL PRIORITY?" board, the green "HATE HAS NO HOME HERE!" sign and the Trump effigy bunch together in front of the lit Beverly Hills sign, lift their placards and the effigy up to camera height and grin straight down the lens. Getting your sign into a news frame is the second reason to point it that way, and it is why the group looks like it is posing rather than merely standing.

3. **The rally is winding down at dusk.** By the closing shots the street lights and the Beverly Hills sign are lit and the sky has gone dark blue. People who were milling loosely about on the grass earlier in the video have consolidated into the kerbside line by the end, so the crowd genuinely is more uniformly aligned at 318 s than it was mid-interview.

## What it is not

It is not a reaction to the woman in white. They are facing outward *past* her, not at her; she simply happens to be standing between the line and the camera, and the anti-Trump crowd behind her largely ignores her. It is not an audience watching a speech or performance, and it is not a confrontation forming — as the shot ends she waves cheerfully at the lens and moves off along the line, with the demonstrators standing calmly behind her, signs still pointed at the traffic, before the copyright card fades in.
